rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.stem: If \(\tan^{-1} x = y\), then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) is equal to :
rows.solution: Differentiate the relation rather than the inverse function. From \(\tan^{-1} x = y\) we get \(x = \tan y\), so \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \sec^2 y\) and therefore \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{\sec^2 y} = \cos^2 y\). This is the familiar result in disguise: since \(\sec^2 y = 1 + \tan^2 y = 1 + x^2\), the derivative equals \(\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}\), and the option offering \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}}\) carries a stray square root. Hence the derivative is \(\cos^2 y\), which is option (D) \(\cos^2 y\).

Clear the negative exponent by substituting \(t = e^{x}\), so that \(dt = e^{x}\,dx\) and \(dx = \dfrac{dt}{t}\). Since \(e^{-2x} = \dfrac{1}{t^2}\), the radical becomes \(\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{t^2} - 1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}{t}\) for \(t > 0\) (the integrand is real only when \(e^{-2x} > 1\), that is \(x < 0\), which is exactly where \(0 < t < 1\)). The integral is therefore \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{dt/t}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}/t} = \int \dfrac{dt}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}} = \sin^{-1} t + C\). Restoring \(t = e^{x}\), the value is \(\sin^{-1}\left(e^{x}\right) + C\), which is option (C) \(\sin^{-1} e^{x} + C\).

rows.stem: Direction ratios of lines \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) respectively are \(<1, -2, 3>\) and \(<-2, p, -6>\). The value of p for which \(l_1 \,\|\, l_2\), is :
rows.solution: Two lines are parallel exactly when their direction ratios are proportional, so \(\dfrac{-2}{1} = \dfrac{p}{-2} = \dfrac{-6}{3}\). The first and third ratios agree, both equalling \(-2\), so the common factor of proportionality is \(-2\). From \(\dfrac{p}{-2} = -2\) we get \(p = 4\). Checking, \(\langle -2, 4, -6 \rangle = -2\langle 1, -2, 3 \rangle\), so the lines are indeed parallel. Hence \(p = 4\), which is option (B) \(4\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.solution: The inverse sine is defined only when its argument lies in \([-1, 1]\), so we need \(-1 \le 1 - 2x \le 1\). Subtracting 1 throughout gives \(-2 \le -2x \le 0\), and dividing by \(-2\) reverses both inequalities to give \(0 \le x \le 1\). Hence the domain is \([0, 1]\), which is option (D) \([0, 1]\).

rows.stem: If a matrix B is such that \(B[1 \;\; 2 \;\; 3] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), then the order of matrix B is :
rows.solution: Use the rule that the product of an \(m \times n\) matrix with an \(n \times p\) matrix is \(m \times p\). Here the second factor \([1 \;\; 2 \;\; 3]\) is a row matrix of order \(1 \times 3\) and the product is a \(3 \times 3\) matrix. So if the matrix B has order \(m \times n\), the product \(B[1 \;\; 2 \;\; 3]\) requires \(n = 1\) for the multiplication to be defined, and its order is then \(m \times 3\). Matching this against \(3 \times 3\) gives \(m = 3\). So the order of the matrix B is \(3 \times 1\), which is option (B) \(3 \times 1\).

rows.subtopic: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
rows.stem: If \(A(\text{adj } A) = \begin{bmatrix} 2026 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2026 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2026 \end{bmatrix}\), then the value of \(|\text{adj } A|\) is equal to :
rows.solution: For any square matrix A of order n, \(A(\text{adj } A) = |A| I\). The given product is \(2026\) times the identity matrix of order 3, so \(|A| = 2026\). Now use \(|\text{adj } A| = |A|^{\,n-1}\); with \(n = 3\) this gives \(|\text{adj } A| = |A|^2 = (2026)^2\). Hence the value is \((2026)^2\), which is option (D) \((2026)^2\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Functions in Parametric Form
rows.stem: If \(x = e^{t + \frac{1}{t}}\) and \(y = e^{t - \frac{1}{t}}\), then find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \(t = -2\).
rows.solution: Differentiate x and y separately with respect to the parameter t. From \(x = e^{t + \frac{1}{t}}\), the chain rule gives \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{t^2}\right)e^{t + \frac{1}{t}}\), and from \(y = e^{t - \frac{1}{t}}\) it gives \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{t^2}\right)e^{t - \frac{1}{t}}\). Dividing, \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \dfrac{1 + \frac{1}{t^2}}{1 - \frac{1}{t^2}} \cdot \dfrac{e^{t - \frac{1}{t}}}{e^{t + \frac{1}{t}}} = \dfrac{t^2 + 1}{t^2 - 1}\, e^{-\frac{2}{t}}\). At \(t = -2\) the first factor is \(\dfrac{4 + 1}{4 - 1} = \dfrac{5}{3}\) and the exponential is \(e^{-2/(-2)} = e\). Hence \(\left[\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right]_{t = -2} = \dfrac{5e}{3}\).

rows.stem: Find the sub-interval of \((0, \infty)\) in which \(f(x) = x^2 e^{-x}\) is increasing.
rows.solution: Differentiate using the product rule: \(f(x) = x^2 e^{-x}\) gives \(f'(x) = 2x e^{-x} - x^2 e^{-x} = x(2 - x)e^{-x}\). Setting \(f'(x) = 0\) gives \(x = 0\) or \(x = 2\). Since \(e^{-x} > 0\) for every x, the sign of \(f'(x)\) is the sign of \(x(2 - x)\); on \((0, \infty)\) this is positive for \(0 < x < 2\) and negative for \(x > 2\). Hence f is increasing on \((0, 2)\). The interval \((0, 2]\) may equally be quoted, since \(f'\) vanishes only at the single endpoint \(x = 2\) and "increasing" is not required to be strict there.

rows.stem: Find the general solution of the differential equation \((x^2 + y^2)\, dy = xy\, dx\).
rows.solution:
Write the equation as \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{xy}{x^2 + y^2}\). The right side is unchanged when x and y are both scaled by the same factor, so the equation is homogeneous. Put \(y = vx\), so that \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\); the right side becomes \(\dfrac{x \cdot vx}{x^2 + v^2x^2} = \dfrac{v}{1 + v^2}\). Hence \(v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v}{1 + v^2}\), that is \(x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v - v\left(1 + v^2\right)}{1 + v^2} = -\dfrac{v^3}{1 + v^2}\).

Separating the variables, \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1 + v^2}{v^3}\,dv = -\int \dfrac{dx}{x}\), that is \(\displaystyle\int\left(v^{-3} + \dfrac{1}{v}\right)dv = -\int \dfrac{dx}{x}\). Integrating gives \(-\dfrac{1}{2v^2} + \log|v| = -\log|x| + c\).

Now restore \(v = \dfrac{y}{x}\): \(\log\left|\dfrac{y}{x}\right| - \dfrac{x^2}{2y^2} = -\log|x| + c\). Since \(\log\left|\dfrac{y}{x}\right| = \log|y| - \log|x|\), the two \(\log|x|\) terms cancel and the general solution simplifies to \(\log|y| = \dfrac{x^2}{2y^2} + c\).

rows.stem: Find the particular solution of the differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} - 3y \cot x = \sin 2x\), given that \(y = 2\) when \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
rows.solution:
The equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} - 3y\cot x = \sin 2x\) is linear in y with \(P = -3\cot x\) and \(Q = \sin 2x\). Its integrating factor is \(e^{\int P\,dx} = e^{-3\int \cot x\,dx} = e^{-3\log|\sin x|} = \dfrac{1}{\sin^3 x} = \operatorname{cosec}^3 x\).

Multiplying through by the integrating factor, the general solution is \(y \operatorname{cosec}^3 x = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sin 2x}{\sin^3 x}\,dx\). Writing \(\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x\), the integrand becomes \(\dfrac{2\sin x\cos x}{\sin^3 x} = \dfrac{2\cos x}{\sin^2 x} = 2\operatorname{cosec} x\cot x\), whose integral is \(-2\operatorname{cosec} x\). Hence \(y\operatorname{cosec}^3 x = -2\operatorname{cosec} x + c\).

Apply the given condition \(y = 2\) when \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), where \(\operatorname{cosec} x = 1\): this gives \(2 = -2 + c\), so \(c = 4\). The particular solution is therefore \(y\operatorname{cosec}^3 x = -2\operatorname{cosec} x + 4\), or equivalently, multiplying by \(\sin^3 x\), \(y = -2\sin^2 x + 4\sin^3 x\).

As a check, differentiating this last form gives \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -4\sin x\cos x + 12\sin^2 x\cos x\), and then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} - 3y\cot x = -4\sin x\cos x + 12\sin^2 x\cos x + 6\sin x\cos x - 12\sin^2 x\cos x = 2\sin x\cos x = \sin 2x\), as required.

Let \(I = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{2^{x} + 1}\,dx\). Apply the property \(\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(a + b - x)\,dx\) with \(a + b = 0\), which replaces x by \(-x\). Since \(\cos^2(-x) = \cos^2 x\) and \(2^{-x} + 1 = \dfrac{1 + 2^{x}}{2^{x}}\), this gives \(I = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{2^{x}\cos^2 x}{2^{x} + 1}\,dx\).

Adding the two expressions for I, the denominators combine and \(2I = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\left(1 + 2^{x}\right)\cos^2 x}{2^{x} + 1}\,dx = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2 x\,dx\). The integrand \(\cos^2 x\) is even, so this equals \(2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^2 x\,dx\), and hence \(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^2 x\,dx\).

Finally, applying \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\,dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) turns cosine into sine, so \(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^2 x\,dx\) as well. Adding these last two expressions, \(2I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left(\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x\right)dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 1\,dx = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Hence \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

rows.stem: Show that \(f : R_+ \to [-5, \infty)\) given by \(f(x) = 4x^2 + 4x - 5\) is both one-one and onto where \(R_+ = [0, \infty)\). Also, find \(p \in R_+\) such that \(f(p) = 3\).
rows.solution:
One-one. Take \(x_1, x_2 \in R_+\) with \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\), that is \(4x_1^2 + 4x_1 - 5 = 4x_2^2 + 4x_2 - 5\). Cancelling the \(-5\) and dividing by 4 gives \(x_1^2 - x_2^2 + x_1 - x_2 = 0\), which factorises as \(\left(x_1 - x_2\right)\left(x_1 + x_2 + 1\right) = 0\). Because \(x_1, x_2 \ge 0\), the second factor satisfies \(x_1 + x_2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0\) and cannot vanish. Hence \(x_1 = x_2\), so f is one-one.

Onto. Let \(y = 4x^2 + 4x - 5\) for some \(y \in [-5, \infty)\) and solve for x. Rearranged, \(4x^2 + 4x - (5 + y) = 0\), so by the quadratic formula \(x = \dfrac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 16(5 + y)}}{8} = \dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{y + 6}}{2}\). Since \(y \ge -5\) we have \(y + 6 \ge 1\), so the square root is real and at least 1; taking the sign that keeps x non-negative gives the pre-image \(x = \dfrac{\sqrt{y + 6} - 1}{2}\), which indeed satisfies \(x \ge 0\) and so lies in \(R_+\). Conversely, for \(x \ge 0\) we have \(\sqrt{y + 6} \ge 1\), that is \(y \ge -5\), so the range is exactly \([-5, \infty)\). Range equals codomain, so f is onto. (Completing the square shows the same thing: \(f(x) = (2x + 1)^2 - 6\), which increases from \(f(0) = -5\) without bound as x runs over \([0, \infty)\).)

Being both one-one and onto, f is a bijection.

Value of p. We need \(f(p) = 3\), that is \(4p^2 + 4p - 5 = 3\), so \(4p^2 + 4p - 8 = 0\) and \(p^2 + p - 2 = 0\). Factorising, \((p + 2)(p - 1) = 0\), giving \(p = 1\) or \(p = -2\). Since \(p \in R_+ = [0, \infty)\), the root \(p = -2\) is rejected and \(p = 1\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following Linear Programming Problem graphically :

Maximise \(Z = 12x + 18y\)

subject to the constraints

\(x + y \le 1200\)

\(x - 2y \ge 0\)

\(x + 3y \ge 600\)

\(x \ge 0,\ y \ge 0\)
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: the corner-point table is headed "Value of Z = 600x + 400y", which is not this paper's objective function; \(600x + 400y\) is the objective of the linear programming question on the sibling paper 65/3/1. Every value tabulated is in fact computed from the objective printed in the question, \(Z = 12x + 18y\) — at \((600, 0)\) it gives 7200, not 360000 — so only the column heading is wrong and the answer \(Z_{\max} = 16800\) at \((800, 400)\) stands.]

Draw the lines \(x + y = 1200\), \(x - 2y = 0\) and \(x + 3y = 600\) in the first quadrant. The line \(x - 2y = 0\) passes through the origin with slope \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), and testing the point \((1, 0)\) shows that \(x - 2y \ge 0\) is the region on and below it. Testing the origin in the other two constraints shows that \(x + y \le 1200\) holds there while \(x + 3y \ge 600\) does not, so the feasible region lies below \(x + y = 1200\) and above \(x + 3y = 600\). Together these give a bounded quadrilateral region.

Its corner points come from intersecting the boundary lines in pairs. The line \(x + 3y = 600\) meets \(y = 0\) at \(A(600, 0)\); the line \(x + y = 1200\) meets \(y = 0\) at \(B(1200, 0)\); the lines \(x + y = 1200\) and \(x = 2y\) meet where \(2y + y = 1200\), giving \(y = 400\) and \(x = 800\), that is \(C(800, 400)\); and the lines \(x = 2y\) and \(x + 3y = 600\) meet where \(2y + 3y = 600\), giving \(y = 120\) and \(x = 240\), that is \(D(240, 120)\). Each of these four points satisfies all of the constraints.

Now evaluate \(Z = 12x + 18y\) at each corner point. At \(A(600, 0)\), \(Z = 7200\); at \(B(1200, 0)\), \(Z = 14400\); at \(C(800, 400)\), \(Z = 9600 + 7200 = 16800\); at \(D(240, 120)\), \(Z = 2880 + 2160 = 5040\).

The feasible region is bounded, so Z attains its maximum at a corner point. Hence \(Z_{\max} = 16800\), attained at the point \((800, 400)\).
